1969 Chevy Corvette Spent 35 Years Parked Until Someone Bought It. Can He Bring It Back to Life?
17 photos
Photo: Classic Performance | YouTube
This 1969 Chevrolet Corvette Stingray spent 35 long years in a garage on a lakefront property. The house was repossessed, and the owner wanted it gone. This is how it ended up in the hands of a classic-car miracle maker. Can he save it and send it back on the road?
The last inspection sticker glued to the cracked windshield dates to 1991 . This means that this car hasn’t been on the road since. Locked away behind a white sliding door, in an underground garage with access to the house on the lakefront property, is a sad sight to behold.
The Corvette Stingray was crashed in the front at some point. With its front end severely contorted, it was parked and never touched again. The owner was probably planning to fix it one day. But that day never came. So, two years ago, when his house was repossessed, he wanted the car off the property.
Parked in his garage, it sat with the fiberglass nose broken, and the bumper and grille badly caved in. The frame was cracked and the internals might have been pushed backward. The windshield is shattered, and the convertible top is torn, but the hidden headlight mechanisms seemed intact.
Photo: Classic Performance | YouTube The 1969 Chevy Corvette is finished in Can-Am White (paint code 972) over a red vinyl Comfortweave interior, with everything original. It sits on the original set of four factory 15 x 8-inch steel Rally wheels, painted black, but they should be Argent Silver.
The car has a trailer hitch, bolted to the rear bumper, as if anyone would tow anything with a Corvette. Probably the owner of this Corvette did. The speedometer was dislocated at some point and shows 34,829 miles (56,062 kilometers), but the man trying to rescue it guesses it’s 134,829 miles (216,986 kilometers).
The car is remarkably unmolested, retaining its original engine, date-code-correct alternator, Quadrajet carburetor, ignition, and correct tach drive distributor. The only piece missing under the hood was the spark plugs, which had mysteriously evaporated. The owner had no idea where they were.
The ‘Vette has the 350-cubic-inch small-block V8 with a four-barrel Rochester Quadrajet carburetor under the hood. The V8 pushes out 300 horsepower (304 metric horsepower) and 380 pound-feet (515 Newton meters) of torque.
Photo: Classic Performance | YouTube That is what makes it accelerate from 0 to 60 mph (0 to 97 kph) in 6.1 seconds and max out at 122 mph (196 kph). A four-speed manual transmission, the purists’ favorite, puts the power down through the rear wheels. Back in 1969, GM was still light-years away from rolling out its first all-wheel-drive Corvette.
However, all those verbs about performance should be in the past tense, because the car doesn’t run, doesn’t drive, has the engine seized and the wheels stuck. Besides, the owner wasn’t going to let it go out without a fight.
He originally asked for $6,000, but the classic car rescuer who went to see it said he would by no means pay more than $3,000 for the beat-up, run-down, badly crashed Corvette. He dragged it out of its long-term entrapment and waited for the call from the owner.
He waited and waited until earlier this year, when the owner finally agreed to the transaction. So here he is, dragging the 1969 Chevy Corvette up on his trailer, with wheels stuck on the right side, leaving deep trails on the ground. Eventually, the one at the back breaks loose, but at a price: the tread on the tire is torn.
Photo: Classic Performance | YouTube The first stop is at the car wash as he is trying to wash off over three decades of abandonment in which this car collected dust instead of miles. Now, it looks miles apart from the car he found two years ago. Once he gets to the shop, he installs new redline tires that he bought on eBay, because there was no way the old rubber could hold air.
To finally break the engine loose and get it to start for the first time in over three decades, its new owner soaked the cylinders in Marvel Mystery Oil for roughly a week. Then, he rolled the Corvette down the trailer and positioned it at the top of a steep hill.
With the transmission shifted into fourth gear, he let the car gain momentum down the hill and repeatedly dropped the clutch. After four to five violent, sudden engagements, the seized engine finally broke free. A piece of painter's tape placed on the engine belt confirmed the motor was spinning freely again.
However, all he gets are a few pops out of the carburetor and exhaust. The compression test brings more bad news, but he is not the one to give up so easily. However, not all "Will it run?" videos end up with an exhaust pipe smoking out all the fury the car collected during decades of sitting parked.
